title: Orchestration Patterns for Reliable Agent Workflows
summary: This intermediate module enables learners to select and explain sequential, routing, parallel, manager-worker, and evaluator-revision patterns for an agent workflow. After completing it, learners can match a workflow structure to task dependencies, uncertainty, and review needs rather than relying on one undifferentiated process.
objectives: Distinguish five orchestration patterns by the way each pattern assigns, orders, and reviews work.
Select a suitable orchestration pattern after identifying task dependencies, opportunities for independent work, and review requirements.
Describe the state, stopping condition, and failure handling that an orchestrator must define.
Explain when additional orchestration complexity is not justified.

sections.title: Level and scope
paragraphs: This is an intermediate-level module. It assumes that you understand that an agent can receive input, perform a bounded task, and return a result. No knowledge of a particular provider, programming language, or orchestration product is required.

Orchestration is the coordination of task order, task assignment, shared state, review, and stopping conditions. In this module, a pattern is a reusable design shape, not a mandatory implementation or a universal taxonomy.

The change affects citation provenance and review metadata. It does not change the module's provider-neutral orchestration guidance. The replacement source supports the broad framing of agent systems as combinations of planning, action, memory, and interaction, while the pattern names below are operational definitions used within this module.

sections.title: Start with task structure
paragraphs: Choose an orchestration pattern only after describing the work. Ask which steps depend on earlier results, which tasks can run independently, whether different inputs require different handling, whether work must be decomposed dynamically, and whether an output requires explicit review.

The orchestrator should maintain only the state needed to coordinate the workflow. Relevant state can include the original request, completed outputs, pending tasks, review feedback, retry counts, and final status. Each transition should have a defined condition so that the workflow does not continue merely because another action is possible.

A stopping condition states when the workflow succeeds, fails, or requires escalation. Examples include completion of all required tasks, acceptance by a reviewer, exhaustion of an allowed retry count, or detection that required information is unavailable.
sections.callout: Use the simplest pattern that represents the real dependencies. Additional agents or branches create more outputs and transitions to coordinate.

sections.title: Sequential pattern
paragraphs: In a sequential pattern, one step produces input for the next step. Use it when order matters, such as when a draft must exist before it can be checked.
The orchestrator records the output of each step, validates that the output is usable, and then passes it forward. If an early result is invalid, later steps should not silently proceed with it.

A sequential workflow is easy to trace because each result has a clear predecessor. Its main limitation is that an early error can propagate through every later step unless a validation or review point catches it.

sections.title: Routing pattern
paragraphs: In a routing pattern, the orchestrator examines an input and selects one of several specialized paths. Use it when different classes of input require different processing.

A route should be based on an explicit condition that can be recorded and inspected. The workflow also needs a fallback for inputs that do not match a route with sufficient confidence or that lack information required for a decision.
Routing differs from sequencing because routing chooses among paths, while sequencing moves through a predetermined order of steps.

sections.title: Parallel pattern
paragraphs: In a parallel pattern, independent tasks are assigned at the same stage and their outputs are later combined. Use it when the tasks do not require one another's intermediate results.

The orchestrator must define what happens if one branch fails or returns late. It must also define how results are merged, including how disagreements, duplicate findings, or missing branch outputs are handled.
Do not use parallel execution when one task needs the result of another. That dependency calls for sequencing, even if other independent parts of the workflow can still run in parallel.

sections.title: Manager-worker pattern
paragraphs: In a manager-worker pattern, a coordinating role decomposes a goal into tasks, assigns those tasks, tracks their status, and combines their results. Use it when the required subtasks cannot be fully enumerated before work begins.

The manager needs boundaries. It should have a limit on task creation, a stopping condition, and a rule for handling overlapping or contradictory worker outputs. Without those controls, decomposition can continue without producing a final result.

This pattern differs from fixed parallel work because the manager can decide during execution which tasks are needed. That flexibility adds coordination cost, so a fixed sequence or fixed set of branches is preferable when the task structure is already known.

sections.title: Evaluator-revision pattern
paragraphs: In an evaluator-revision pattern, one step produces an output, another assesses it against stated criteria, and the output may be revised using the feedback. Use it when quality can be judged against explicit requirements and revision is permitted.
The evaluator should return actionable findings tied to the criteria. A vague rejection does not tell the revision step what to change.

The loop needs a stopping rule, such as acceptance, a revision limit, or escalation when the same problem persists. A review loop without a stopping rule can repeat without resolving the underlying issue.

sections.title: Select and compose patterns
paragraphs: Select sequencing when outputs have strict dependencies. Select routing when inputs require different paths. Select parallel work when tasks are independent. Select manager-worker coordination when decomposition must adapt during execution. Select evaluator-revision when an output must be checked and can be improved using specific feedback.

A workflow can compose patterns. For example, it can route an input, run independent checks in parallel within the selected route, merge the results, and then evaluate the merged output. Each composition point must define its input, output, state transition, and failure behavior.

Before implementation, write down the task graph, required state, stopping conditions, fallback paths, and review criteria. This makes it possible to determine whether the selected structure matches the work and whether every possible path can terminate.

questions.prompt: A workflow must send different classes of input through different specialized paths. Which pattern directly addresses this requirement?
choices: Sequential
Routing
Parallel
Evaluator-revision
questions.explanation: Routing examines an input and selects a specialized path according to an explicit condition.

questions.prompt: When is the parallel pattern appropriate?
choices: When every task requires the previous task's result
When independent tasks can be performed at the same stage and later combined
When an output must always be revised
When no stopping condition can be defined
questions.explanation: Parallel orchestration is appropriate when tasks do not require one another's intermediate results and their outputs can later be combined.

questions.prompt: What distinguishes the manager-worker pattern from a fixed set of parallel branches?
choices: The manager can determine during execution which subtasks are needed
The manager removes the need for stopping conditions
Workers must all perform the same task
Worker results never need to be combined
questions.explanation: The manager-worker pattern supports adaptive decomposition, allowing the coordinating role to decide during execution which subtasks are required.

questions.prompt: What must an evaluator-revision loop include to avoid repeating indefinitely?
choices: An unlimited number of revisions
A stopping rule such as acceptance, a revision limit, or escalation
A requirement that every output be rejected once
Independent branches with no merge rule
questions.explanation: The module states that evaluator-revision loops need a stopping rule, such as acceptance, a revision limit, or escalation.

questions.prompt: What should a designer identify before selecting an orchestration pattern?
choices: Task dependencies, independent work, routing needs, and review requirements
The largest possible number of agents
A way to avoid recording state
A process with no failure path
questions.explanation: Pattern selection begins by describing the work, including dependencies, independent tasks, differing input paths, dynamic decomposition, and review needs.
